newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila seen reaping rewards by sheltering defector.
newsitem.headline: Manila seen reaping rewards by sheltering defector.

text.p: The decision to shelter North Korean defector Hwang Jang-yop leaves Beijing owing Manila a favour, a situation which could bring the Philippines long-term political benefits, analysts and diplomats said on Wednesday.
By helping its giant neighbour out of a tricky situation, the Philippines gains tremendous leverage in future relations with Asia's diplomatic heavyweight -- China, the analysts said.
"This takes a bone out of China's throat," a senior Filipino political analyst said.

Hwang, who defected from his Stalinist homeland on February 12 while on a visit to China, arrived in the Philippines on Tuesday in an arrangement requiring him to go to a third country before landing in Seoul to placate North Korean authorities.

By operating as the third country, Manila also strengthens its relations with Seoul, one of the region's most dynamic economies and one of two Asian members of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development club of rich nations.

But the possible economic and political benefits do not come without any risks as diplomats and analysts closely watch how the Philippines handles the delicate security arrangements associated with Hwang's visit. Hwang's hideaway in the Philippines, for example, is a fiercely guarded secret which military officials said reflected fears of an assassination attempt by North Korean hitmen.
President Fidel Ramos said on Wednesday in his weekly news conference that Hwang was in the Philippines, the first official admission that Pyongyang's top ideologue was in the country.
But he firmly declined to answer further questions.
"I will not make any further comment in view of the fact that the security of our visitor is of paramount interest," he said.
As part of an economic reform programme, the Philippines has given priority to better foreign trade relations and officials consider China a key market.
"It really improves the Philippines' relations with China and its long-term benefits will be immense," a Western diplomat said.
The Philippines and China are also in a dispute over competing claims on the potentially oil-rich Spratlys islands, a cluster of reefs in the South China Sea.

But questions over Hwang's safety in the Philippines have surrounded the visit. The country is notorious for its high number of kidnappings, daring daylight bank robberies, and allegations of police corruption.
A recent issue of the U.S. magazine Fortune called the Philippines "the kidnapping capital of Asia."
But a Western diplomat dismissed the suggestion that Hwang could be in danger.
"The Presidential Security Guard is as good as any and if they are protecting him, there should be no fear," he said.
The Filipino political analyst, who did not want to be named, said the Philippines may have decided to shelter Hwang at the urging of the United States.
"I think there was strong pressure from Washington and the Philippines agreed because even if the bases have gone, there are strong relations between the two countries," he said.
"Both South Korea and the Philippines have strong lines with America," one Asian diplomat said.
Until 1992, the Philippines hosted two major U.S. military bases, including the Subic Bay naval base, the largest U.S. facility overseas.
Talk of U.S. involvement in Hwang's clandestine arrival started on Tuesday when some officials said he was at a U.S. consular facility in Manila.
